flashcards.q: What was the root cause of Knight Capital's 2012 $440M loss, precisely?
flashcards.a: A deployment script failed silently to update 1 of 8 trading servers but reported success; the unpatched server ran dormant 2003-era code that misinterpreted a repurposed flag bit, triggering runaway trading â€” 4M unintended orders, ~$7B in unwanted positions, ~$440M lost in 45 minutes.

flashcards.q: What caused the AWS US-EAST-1 outage of October 20, 2025?
flashcards.a: A latent race condition in DynamoDB's internal DNS management system corrupted DNS records for critical endpoints, cascading into failures across dozens of AWS services for 14-15 hours.

flashcards.q: What caused the Cloudflare global outage of November 18, 2025?
flashcards.a: A Bot Management configuration change doubled the size of a 'feature file' used by the traffic-proxy software, exceeding a hard-coded size limit and crashing proxy processes globally and near-simultaneously since config propagated worldwide without staged rollout.

flashcards.q: What's the common structural pattern across the AWS Oct 2025 and Cloudflare Nov 2025 outages?
flashcards.a: Both were control-plane bugs/misconfigurations (DNS record management; a bot-mgmt feature file) that propagated globally rather than being contained by region/scope, because the control plane prioritized fast global consistency over blast-radius containment.

flashcards.q: Describe GitHub's October 2018 incident in CAP-theorem terms.
flashcards.a: A 43-second network partition made the failover orchestrator believe the primary was down (from a single node's local view) and promoted a second primary, choosing availability over consistency. Two primaries both accepted writes; reconciliation took 24+ hours.

flashcards.q: What's the fix for GitHub's split-brain failure mode, precisely?
flashcards.a: Quorum-based failover requiring agreement from multiple independent observers before promoting a new primary, rather than a single node's local 'I can't reach the primary' view â€” reduces but doesn't eliminate the risk of promoting during a transient partition.

flashcards.q: What did Prime Video's 2023 monolith move actually apply to, and what result did it produce?
flashcards.a: One internal service (Video Quality Analysis monitoring), not the whole platform â€” moved from Step Functions/Lambda/S3-hop orchestration to a single ECS task with in-memory data passing, cutting infrastructure cost over 90% and increasing scaling capacity. Rest of Prime Video stayed microservices.

flashcards.q: Why is 'Prime Video proves microservices are bad' a misreading of the case study?
flashcards.a: The change was scoped to one service whose workload was a tight, sequentially-dependent processing pipeline â€” exactly the shape where orchestration/inter-hop overhead dominates. The lesson is matching granularity to workload coordination pattern, not a blanket verdict against microservices.

flashcards.q: What did Segment's 2020 'Goodbye Microservices' consolidation keep, and what did it give up?
flashcards.a: Kept clear internal module boundaries per integration (still modular); gave up full process-level separation (hundreds of per-integration services), since most needed failure isolation was achievable in-process via timeouts/circuit breakers per destination.

flashcards.q: When is full process-level service separation actually worth its operational cost, per the Segment lesson?
flashcards.a: When components genuinely need independent scaling or independent team ownership â€” not merely fault isolation, which is often achievable in-process at lower operational cost (fewer deploy pipelines, less on-call surface).

flashcards.q: What remediation did both AWS and Cloudflare publicly commit to after their 2025 incidents?
flashcards.a: Staged/canary rollout discipline for control-plane and configuration changes (not just code deploys), with health-check gates before wider propagation, rather than instantaneous global broadcast.

flashcards.q: Why didn't downstream circuit breakers save AWS's and Cloudflare's customers during the 2025 outages?
flashcards.a: A breaker still needs to reach the dependency (or its health check) to decide whether to trip; when the control-plane failure breaks the addressing/discovery layer itself (DNS, proxy fleet), the breaker's own health-check path degrades along with the thing it's meant to protect against.

flashcards.q: What's the minimum viable retrofit to add blast-radius containment to an existing global control plane?
flashcards.a: A canary tier (small fleet %/one low-traffic region) that receives every push first, gated behind automated health signals with a bake time before wider rollout, plus rollback faster than full propagation â€” a checkpoint insertion, not a rearchitecture.

flashcards.q: What did Google's SRE book (2016) formalize, and why did it matter for postmortem quality?
flashcards.a: The 'blameless postmortem' â€” removing the incentive to stay vague to avoid blaming an individual, which made it safe to publish the actual mechanical failure chain in enough detail to be useful to people who weren't there, including future readers of the case study.
